name: Building Data Dashboards (Power BI and Data Studio)
objectives: Given a business need such as "Which products sell best?", write a one-sentence dashboard question, name the audience and choose 3 to 5 key numbers (KPIs), with each key number's name, how it is calculated and its time period
Given a messy practice sales sheet, clean the data into a tidy table with one row per record and one column per field, with no blank headers, no duplicate rows and one format for each column

Given a question about a trend, a comparison or a share of a total, choose and build the chart type that fits the question in Power BI Desktop or Data Studio, getting at least 4 of 5 chart choices right

Using your cleaned data in Power BI Desktop or Data Studio, build a one-page dashboard with key number cards, at least 2 charts, a date filter and one other filter, so a viewer can answer the dashboard question in under one minute
Given a finished dashboard and its source data, check at least 3 totals on the dashboard against the source data and fix any that do not match, before anyone else sees it
When your dashboard is ready, share or export the dashboard with view-only access and write a 3-sentence summary of what it shows, without sharing any private data

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Planning the dashboard and getting the data ready

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Starting with the question and the key numbers
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a dashboard question, name its audience and choose 3 to 5 key numbers.
This lesson builds toward: Given a business need such as "Which products sell best?", you will write a one-sentence dashboard question, name the audience and choose 3 to 5 key numbers (KPIs), with each key number's name, how it is calculated and its time period.
A dashboard is one screen of numbers and charts that helps someone make a decision. A good one starts with a question, not with a chart. Ask: who will look at this, and what do they need to decide?
Example: the owner of a small bakery asks, "Which products and which days bring in the most money each month?" The audience is the owner. The decision is what to bake more of and when to schedule staff.
Next, pick 3 to 5 key numbers, called KPIs. For the bakery: total sales in dollars, number of items sold, average sale per order, and the best-selling product. Write how each is calculated and for what time period, for example "Total sales = sum of the Total column, this month".
Too many numbers hide the important ones. If a number does not help answer the question, leave it off.
Step by step:
- Name the audience: who will use the dashboard?
- Write the question in one sentence.
- Name the decision it helps them make.
- Choose 3 to 5 key numbers that answer it.
- For each, write its name, how it is calculated and its time period.
Words to know:
- Dashboard: one screen of key numbers and charts that helps someone make a decision.
- KPI (key performance indicator): one of the few numbers that shows whether things are going well, like total sales this month.
- Audience: the people who will look at the dashboard.
- Metric: any number you measure, like items sold or average sale.
Official sources:
- Microsoft Learn: Power BI Data Analyst Associate (exam PL-300)
- CompTIA Data+ (exam DA0-002)
Try it now: Pick a job you want (for example warehouse, clinic front desk, store manager or the bakery example). On paper, write the audience, the one-sentence question, the decision, and 3 to 5 key numbers with how each is calculated and the time period. Keep this page: it is the plan for your final dashboard.
You can now write a dashboard question for a real audience and choose 3 to 5 key numbers that answer it.

check.q: What should you do FIRST when you build a dashboard?
options: Write the question and who it is for
Add every chart the tool offers
check.why: The question and audience decide which numbers and charts belong on the page.

check.q: Which is the best key number for "Which products bring in the most money each month?"
options: Total sales in dollars by product, this month
check.why: Sales by product for the month directly answers the question.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Cleaning data into a tidy table
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Clean a messy sheet into a tidy table with one row per record and one column per field.
This lesson builds toward: Given a messy practice sales sheet, you will clean the data into a tidy table with one row per record and one column per field, with no blank headers, no duplicate rows and one format for each column.
Dashboard tools work best with a tidy table: one header row, one row for each record (each sale, each order) and one column for each field (Date, Product, Units). No merged cells, no blank rows, no totals typed inside the data.
Messy data gives wrong numbers. Common problems: the same sale typed twice (a duplicate), blank cells, dates written different ways (10/3/26 and Oct 3), numbers stored as text ("$4.50" typed with a space), and spelling differences ("Muffin" and "muffins").
In Google Sheets you can fix most of this: Data > Data cleanup > Remove duplicates, Format > Number to set dates and currency, and Edit > Find and replace to fix spellings. Keep the original sheet and clean a copy, so you can always go back.
Practice data for this course (made up): columns Date, Product, Category, Units, Price, Total. For example 10/1/2026, Muffin, Pastry, 12, 2.50, 30.00.
Step by step:
- Make a copy of the sheet and work on the copy.
- Make sure there is exactly one header row with a clear name in every column.
- Remove blank rows, merged cells and any total rows inside the data.
- Remove duplicate rows.
- Give each column one format: dates as dates, money as currency, text spelled the same way.
- Check one row by hand: Units times Price should equal Total.
Words to know:
- Tidy table: data with one header row, one row per record and one column per field.
- Record: one row of data, like one sale.
- Field: one column of data, like Date or Product.
- Duplicate: the same record typed twice.
- Data type: what kind of value a column holds: number, date, currency or text.
Official sources:
- Google Docs Editors Help: Split text, remove duplicates, or trim whitespace
Try it now: In Google Sheets, type 15 rows of made-up bakery sales (Date, Product, Category, Units, Price, Total) over two weeks. On purpose, add 1 duplicate row, 1 blank row, 1 date written as text (Oct 5) and 1 spelling difference ("muffins"). Then make a copy and clean it with the steps. Count how many problems you fixed.
You can now spot and fix duplicates, blanks, mixed formats and spelling differences to make a tidy table.

check.q: Your sheet shows "Muffin" and "muffins" as two products. What do you do?
options: Leave it; the tool will guess
Use Find and replace so every row says "Muffin"
check.why: One spelling per item means the tool adds them together correctly.

options: Merged title cells over the data
One header row, one row per record, one column per field
A total row in the middle of the data
Two header rows with blank cells
check.why: Dashboard tools read tidy tables correctly; merged cells and typed totals confuse them.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Loading data into Power BI Desktop or Data Studio
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Load a tidy table into Power BI Desktop or Data Studio and check each column's data type.
This lesson builds toward: Given a messy practice sales sheet, you will clean the data into a tidy table with one row per record and one column per field, with no blank headers, no duplicate rows and one format for each column.
Choose your tool. Power BI Desktop is free from Microsoft and runs on a Windows computer. Looker Studio, which Google now calls Data Studio, is free and runs in a web browser, so it works on a Mac, a Chromebook or a library computer. Both are used in real jobs; the skills move from one to the other.
Power BI Desktop: download it only from Microsoft's official site. Save your clean sheet as an Excel or CSV file. Choose Get data, pick the file, and look at the preview. Choose Transform data if a column needs fixing; this opens the Power Query Editor, where you can set a column's data type.
Data Studio: sign in with a Google account, choose Create, then Data source, choose the Google Sheets connector, pick your spreadsheet and worksheet, and choose Connect. You will see your fields listed with their types.
In both tools, check every column: Date should be a date, Units and Total should be numbers, Product should be text. A number stored as text cannot be added up. Fields you count or add (Units, Total) are often called measures or metrics; fields you group by (Product, Date) are called dimensions.
Step by step:
- Pick Power BI Desktop (Windows) or Data Studio (any browser).
- Power BI: Get data, pick your Excel or CSV file, look at the preview, choose Load or Transform data.
- Data Studio: Create, Data source, Google Sheets connector, pick the sheet, Connect.
- Check each column's type: dates, numbers, text.
- Fix any wrong type before you build charts.
Words to know:
- Power BI Desktop: a free Microsoft program for Windows that builds reports and dashboards.
- Data Studio (Looker Studio): Google's free browser tool for reports and dashboards; Google renamed Looker Studio to Data Studio.
- Data source: the file or sheet a dashboard reads its data from.
- Power Query Editor: the part of Power BI where you clean and shape data before building visuals.
- Dimension: a field you group by, like Product or Date.
- Measure (metric): a number you add, count or average, like Total sales.
- CSV file: a plain text file of data with values separated by commas.
Official sources:
- Microsoft: Power BI Desktop (free download)
- Google Cloud: Data Studio (formerly Looker Studio) help
- Google Cloud: Connect Data Studio to Google Sheets
Try it now: Load your cleaned bakery sheet into Power BI Desktop or Data Studio. Write down each column and its data type. If any number shows as text, fix it in the tool or in the sheet, then reload. Then name which fields are dimensions and which are measures.
You can now load a tidy table into Power BI Desktop or Data Studio and make sure every column has the right data type.

check.q: Your Total column loaded as text. What happens if you leave it?
options: The tool cannot add the totals up correctly
Nothing; text and numbers work the same
check.why: Only number columns can be summed or averaged.

check.q: You only have a Chromebook. Which tool can you use for this course?
options: Data Studio in the web browser
check.why: Data Studio runs in a browser; Power BI Desktop needs Windows.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Choosing the right chart
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose and build the chart that fits each kind of question.
This lesson builds toward: Given a question about a trend, a comparison or a share of a total, you will choose and build the chart type that fits the question in Power BI Desktop or Data Studio, getting at least 4 of 5 chart choices right.
Match the chart to the question. A change over time (sales by day or month) is a line chart. A comparison between groups (sales by product) is a bar or column chart, sorted from biggest to smallest. Parts of a whole (share of sales by category) can be a pie or donut chart, but only with a few slices; a bar chart is often clearer.
One key number on its own is a card in Power BI or a scorecard in Data Studio. Exact values people need to look up go in a table. A map only helps when location matters.
To build: in Power BI Desktop, click a visual in the Visualizations pane, then drag a dimension (Product) and a measure (Total) into its fields. In Data Studio, choose Add a chart, pick the type, then set the dimension and the metric.
Keep charts honest: bar charts start at zero, every chart has a clear title that says what it shows ("Sales by product, October"), and you use one color unless color means something.
Step by step:
- Read the question: is it about time, comparing groups, parts of a whole, or one number?
- Time: line chart. Compare: bar chart, sorted. Parts: pie with few slices, or a bar. One number: card or scorecard.
- Add the chart and set the dimension and the measure.
- Give it a title that says what it shows and the time period.
- Check that bars start at zero.
Words to know:
- Line chart: a chart that shows how a number changes over time.
- Bar chart: a chart of bars that compares groups; column charts are bar charts standing up.
- Pie chart: a circle cut into slices that shows parts of a whole.
- Card / scorecard: a box that shows one big number, such as total sales.
- Visual: Power BI's word for a chart, card, table or map.
Official sources:
- CompTIA Data+ (exam DA0-002)
- Microsoft Learn: Power BI Data Analyst Associate (exam PL-300)
Try it now: Using your bakery data, build three charts: (1) total sales by date as a line chart, (2) total sales by product as a bar chart sorted biggest first, (3) total sales as one card or scorecard. Give each a clear title. Then write one sentence each chart tells you.
You can now choose a line, bar, pie, card or table to fit a question and build it with a clear title.

check.q: Which chart best shows how sales changed each day this month?
check.why: Line charts show change over time.

check.q: You want to compare sales across 8 products. Which is clearest?
options: A bar chart sorted from biggest to smallest
check.why: A sorted bar chart makes comparisons easy; 8 pie slices are hard to read.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Laying out the dashboard with cards and filters
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a one-page dashboard with key number cards, charts, a date filter and one other filter.
This lesson builds toward: Using your cleaned data in Power BI Desktop or Data Studio, you will build a one-page dashboard with key number cards, at least 2 charts, a date filter and one other filter, so a viewer can answer the dashboard question in under one minute.
People read a screen from the top left. Put the key number cards in a row across the top, the most important chart under them, and details lower down. Add a title for the whole page and the date range it covers.
Filters let viewers change what they see. In Power BI they are called slicers: add a Slicer visual and put Date in it, then add another for Category. In Data Studio they are called controls: choose Add a control, pick Date range control, then add a Drop-down list control for Category.
Test the filters: pick one category and make sure every card and chart changes. If one does not, it is not connected to the same data.
Leave white space, line things up, and remove anything that does not help answer the question. Then do the one-minute test: show the page to a friend and ask the dashboard question. Can they answer it in under a minute?
Step by step:
- Add a page title and the date range.
- Put 3 to 5 key number cards in a row across the top.
- Put the main chart under the cards and other charts below.
- Add a date filter (slicer or date range control).
- Add one more filter, such as Category.
- Test: change each filter and watch every card and chart change.
- Do the one-minute test with another person.
Words to know:
- Layout: where each card and chart sits on the page.
- Filter: a control that lets the viewer show only some of the data, like one month.
- Slicer: Power BI's name for a filter on the page.
- Control: Data Studio's name for a filter on the page, like a date range control.
Official sources:
- Microsoft: Power BI Desktop (free download)
- Google Cloud: Data Studio (formerly Looker Studio) help
Try it now: Put your three charts from Lesson 4 on one page. Add at least one more key number card (for example items sold or average sale), a date filter and a Category filter. Line everything up. Then ask someone your dashboard question and time how long they take to answer from the page.
You can now lay out a one-page dashboard with key number cards, charts and working filters that someone can read in under a minute.

check.q: Where should the key number cards usually go?
options: In a row across the top
check.why: People read from the top left, so key numbers go first.

check.q: You pick one category in the filter, but one chart does not change. What does that mean?
options: That chart is not connected to the same data or filter
check.why: Every card and chart should respond; one that does not needs to be fixed.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Checking the numbers and sharing safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check 3 dashboard totals against the source data, then share it view-only with a short summary.
This lesson builds toward: Given a finished dashboard and its source data, you will check at least 3 totals on the dashboard against the source data and fix any that do not match, before anyone else sees it. When your dashboard is ready, you will share or export the dashboard with view-only access and write a 3-sentence summary of what it shows, without sharing any private data.
A dashboard is only useful if it can be trusted. Before anyone sees it, check at least 3 numbers. Example: the card says total sales were $1,240. In your sheet, use SUM on the Total column for the same dates. Do they match? Then check one product and one day the same way.
If a number does not match, look for the usual causes: a filter is still set, duplicates came back, a column is text instead of a number, the date range is different, or the card uses Count instead of Sum.
Share safely. In Data Studio, use the Share button and give people view access, not edit access. With Power BI Desktop, export the page to PDF or save the file and send it only to the right person; publishing online may need a work or school account. Never put real customer, patient or employee details in a practice dashboard.
Add a 3-sentence summary: what the dashboard shows, the most important finding, and one suggested action. Example: "This shows bakery sales for October. Muffins earned the most, and Saturdays were the busiest day. We could bake more muffins and add one staff member on Saturdays."
Step by step:
- Clear all filters.
- Check 3 numbers against the source sheet: the total, one product and one day.
- If one is wrong, check filters, duplicates, data types, dates, and Sum vs Count.
- Share with view-only access, or export to PDF.
- Write a 3-sentence summary: what it shows, the main finding, one action.
Words to know:
- Validate: check that a number is right by comparing it with the source.
- View-only access: people can look at the dashboard but cannot change it.
- Export: save a copy in another format, such as PDF.
- Insight: a useful finding that helps someone decide what to do.
Official sources:
- Google Cloud: Data Studio (formerly Looker Studio) help
- CompTIA Data+ (exam DA0-002)
Try it now: Finish your final task: check 3 numbers on your dashboard against your sheet and write down each pair. Fix any mismatch. Then share it view-only (Data Studio) or export a PDF (Power BI), and write your 3-sentence summary. Score yourself with the rubric before you call it done.
You can now check a dashboard's numbers against its source, share it safely, and explain what it shows in three sentences.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Question and key numbers No clear question, or more than 5 numbers with no time period. One-sentence question, audience named, 3 to 5 key numbers each with how it is calculated and a time period. Also names the decision the dashboard supports and why each number matters to it. Tidy data Duplicates, blank rows, mixed date formats or numbers stored as text remain. One header row, one row per record, correct data types, no duplicates. Keeps the original sheet and a short note of every fix made. Right charts Chart types do not fit the questions, or titles are missing. At least 2 charts that fit their questions, with clear titles; bars start at zero. Can explain why each chart type was chosen over another. Layout and filters Cards are missing, or filters do not update every visual. 3 or more key number cards at the top, a date filter and one other filter that update everything; passes the one-minute test. Clean, lined-up layout with nothing extra; a viewer answers in well under a minute. Numbers checked No numbers checked against the source. 3 numbers checked and written down; any mismatch fixed. Explains the cause of a mismatch they found and how they fixed it. Shared safely with a summary Shared with edit access, contains private data, or no summary. Shared view-only or exported to PDF, no private data, 3-sentence summary with a finding and an action. Summary is ready to read aloud in a job interview as a portfolio piece. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check it again.

check.q: Your card says 340 items sold, but SUM of Units in the sheet says 310. What should you check first?
options: Whether a filter is set or duplicates came back
check.why: Filters and duplicates are common causes of totals that do not match.

check.q: Your manager only needs to look at the dashboard. What access do you give?
check.why: View-only lets them see it without changing it by accident.
